stops.name: Hadrumetum, landfall after thirty-six years
stops.campa: The fleet raises the African coast and he steps ashore at Hadrumetum, south of Carthage: a boy of nine when he left this country, a one-eyed man of forty-four returning with the wreck of an empire to save. He does not go up to Carthage; he builds an army instead, folding his Italian veterans, the men of Cannae, grey now, around new levies and Numidian horse bought with whatever Numidia will still sell. Rome's war has come home to the land where the oath was sworn.

stops.name: The plain of Naraggara, the parley of the two captains
stops.campa: Between the two camps, on ground Scipio has chosen and Hannibal has accepted, the two greatest soldiers of the age ride out, one interpreter apiece, and meet for the first time. For a moment, Polybius says, they look at each other in silence, in wonder. Hannibal speaks first: the elder, the invader, the man who has seen fortune from both sides. He offers peace and speaks of chance; Scipio answers that the time for terms was before he crossed to Africa. They part with courtesy and no agreement, each knowing the other told the truth. Tomorrow the world will be decided by professionals who respect each other completely.
stops.quote: The best fortune would have been that Rome had never desired anything beyond Italy, nor Carthage beyond Africa. A certain peace is better and safer than a hoped-for victory: the one is in your own power, the other in the hands of the gods.
stops.quote_source: Livy 30.30; Polybius 15.6-7, Hannibal to Scipio at the parley before Zama

stops.name: Zama, the last field
stops.campa: Eighty elephants open the battle, and Scipio opens lanes and blows them through with trumpets. Massinissa's Numidians, Hannibal's own weapon his whole life, ride this day for Rome and strip the Carthaginian flanks. Line by line the army is spent until only the third stands: the veterans of Italy, held back for the end, fighting to a standstill until the Roman cavalry returns at their backs: Cannae inverted, executed on its inventor. Twenty thousand fall. Hannibal cuts his way out and rides for Hadrumetum, having done, Polybius judges, everything a great general could do. The field itself the canon never fixes; the register holds the tradition.

stops.name: Carthage, the tears and the laughter
stops.campa: He enters Carthage after thirty-six years as the advocate of surrender. When Gisgo rises in the assembly to argue against the peace, Hannibal, a soldier ignorant, he admits, of city manners, drags him from the rostrum, then apologizes: he left this city at nine; let them pardon a man who grew up in a camp. When the terms are read and the senators weep, he laughs aloud, and answers their fury like a surgeon: the time for weeping was when the arms were surrendered and the ships burned; they cry now because the wound has reached their purses. Carthage takes the peace, and takes the man.
stops.quote: If one could see the state's inward mind as one sees a face, this laughter would not seem to you the laughter of joy but of a heart half-mad with its miseries. The time for your tears was when our arms were taken from us and our ships were burned; you weep now because the loss touches your own purses.
stops.quote_source: Livy 30.44 (condensed), Hannibal to the weeping senate of Carthage

stops.name: Byrsa, the suffete against the Hundred and Four
stops.campa: Carthage elects the beaten general suffete, and the oligarchs learn that the breaker of armies breaks account-books too. He audits the state and finds the Roman tribute stolen twice over by its collectors; and when the Hundred and Four, life-tenured judges, the shadow senate that crucifies generals, shield the thieves, he carries a law before the people making the judges elected year by year, none twice running. In one summer he unmakes the oligarchy and pays the indemnity from recovered graft, no new tax. The Hundred and Four do what Rome could not: they write to the senate that Hannibal plots with Antiochus, and the commissioners sail.

stops.name: The tower by the sea, between Acylla and Thapsus
stops.campa: The Roman commissioners land pretending other business, and Hannibal does not wait for the pretense to ripen. He shows himself in the forum until evening, then rides out of Carthage in the dark with two companions, changing horses through the night, and by morning is at his own tower on the coast between Acylla and Thapsus, where, because he has expected exile for years, a ship lies provisioned with a crew that asks nothing. The greatest citizen Carthage ever produced leaves her forever between a sunset and a sunrise, a fugitive from his own countrymen more than from Rome.

stops.name: Cercina, the tent of sails
stops.campa: At Cercina the harbor is full of Phoenician merchantmen, any one of which could carry word to Carthage before him. Recognized at once, he announces he is an envoy bound for Tyre, and invites every shipmaster to a feast on the beach; and since it is midsummer, might they not lend their sails and yards for shade? The awning goes up, made of every sail in the harbor; the wine goes late. In the first dark of morning his ship slips out alone. The masters wake at noon under their own borrowed canvas, hours of rigging from any pursuit. He has escaped an island with a dinner party.

stops.name: Tyre, the mother city
stops.campa: He sails east along the whole spine of the sea to Tyre, the mother of Carthage, and the founders' city receives the exile as a son of the house come home: the canon says he was welcomed with every honor, as if born there. In the temple of Melqart of Tyre, the original fire of which Gades and Carthage burn copies, the circle closes on itself: Dido sailed west from this rock to found the city that raised him; her city has cast him out; the first city takes him back. He rests, and the east begins to learn what the west could not hold.

stops.name: Ephesus: the court of Antiochus, and the oath retold
stops.campa: At Ephesus he joins Antiochus the Great, the one king with weight enough to be Rome's counterpoise, and the king acquires both a weapon and a problem: Roman envoys make a show of long friendly visits to Hannibal, and the poison works: Antiochus cools. So Hannibal tells the king the one story that cannot be doubted: the altar at Carthage, his father's hand, the oath of a nine-year-old kept for fifty years. Antiochus hears it and believes, and the suspicion dies. Later, reviewing his gilded, jewel-crusted army, the king asks whether all this will be enough for the Romans, and receives the canon's most expensive joke.
stops.quote: Yes, quite enough for the Romans, I think — even though they are the greediest men alive.
stops.quote_source: Aulus Gellius 5.5, Hannibal to Antiochus reviewing the gilded army; the oath retold: Polybius 3.11

stops.name: Ephesus, the second meeting with Scipio
stops.campa: Scipio Africanus comes east with an embassy, and the two old enemies meet again: no armies now, two middle-aged men walking and talking. Who was the greatest general? Alexander, says Hannibal: with a small army he routed innumerable hosts and reached the world's ends. Second? Pyrrhus: no man ever chose ground better. Third? Myself. Scipio laughs: and if you had beaten me? The answer is the most perfect courtesy ever paid inside a boast; the canon of three nations keeps it. That season, after the philosopher Phormio lectures him on war for hours, Hannibal remarks he has seen many old madmen: none madder than Phormio.
stops.quote: Then, had I beaten you, I should have placed myself before Alexander, before Pyrrhus, before all.
stops.quote_source: Livy 35.14; Plutarch, Flamininus 21; Appian, Syriaca 10, the generals exchange. Phormio: Cicero, De Oratore 2.75

stops.name: Off Side, the sea-fight at the Eurymedon
stops.campa: Antiochus, taking none of his plan to carry the war to Italy itself as Hannibal had urged, gives him instead a fleet, the one weapon he has never wielded. Off Side, near the mouth of the Eurymedon, Hannibal commands at sea for the only time in his life, against the Rhodians, the finest sailors afloat. His own wing presses theirs and breaks ships; the Rhodian center and left shatter the Seleucid line, and the day is lost. It is the single defeat of his career before Zama's shadow-country, and the register records it without flinching: the god of Tyre gave him the land, and the sea he gave to Rhodes.

stops.name: Gortyn, Crete: the gold in the statues
stops.campa: After Magnesia breaks Antiochus, the peace names Hannibal for surrender, and he vanishes to Gortyn on Crete. He arrives rich, and Cretans notice riches. So he fills amphorae with lead, crusts the tops with gold and silver, and deposits them in Diana's temple with grave ceremony, before witnesses, entrusting his fortune to Gortynian honor. The town posts a guard on the temple: watching, above all, Hannibal. His actual gold he pours into battered bronze statues tumbled like junk in his courtyard. When he sails he carries his trash and leaves the Cretans faithfully guarding his lead. The old lion, the canon smiles, out-foxes a whole island.
